https://friedhats.com/products/colombia-.lines:
Our absolutely epic run of lots from Sebastian Gomez is coming to an end; starting with the caturra, then the natural gesha, then the EF2 gesha, and finally this EF2 gesha competition lot. This lot was set aside, a noticeable notch above the rest, and saved to end the releases from this harvest. The Sebastian Gomez EF2 has seemingly become a perennial feature of the Friedhats menu, so what exactly is EF2? Let’s get into it a bit.
EF2 is an umbrella term that our friends at Cofinet use to classify coffees that undergo an extensive form of fermentation. In this instance, Sebastian begins with the cherries fermenting openly for 24 hours before moving into sealed grainpro bags for 50 hours, kept below 22 degrees for the duration of the fermentation, before being dried on raised beds. This processing helps deliver the signature cane sugar sweetness and syrupy body of this Gesha that we have come to adore. In this lot you will immediately notice an even more explosive complexity bursting with grape juice and macerated mango.

For this microlot the coffee underwent 72 hours of fermentation in sealed plastic tanks before drying in solar tents between 25-40 days.

https://friedhats.com/products/colombia-.lines:
When Wilmer took over the farm from his parents, it had exclusively grown Typica and Caturra since at least their purchase of the land in 1967. Over the past 6 years he ambitiously replaced all of the existing trees with Tabi, Gesha, Pink Bourbon, and Papayo- a massive undertaking. Now with all 6 hectares of his land freshly populated with new varieties, he has turned his eye to experimenting with processing.
When Dylan visited Finca La Loma he committed to buying an experimental salt natural lot from Wilmer if he was willing to try it with the Papayo varietal, giving a purchase guarantee so the risk of trial would be limited, and we’re all glad he did! For this lot, harvested cherries are held in a container with water and 2% salt by weight- what some may recognize as the standard approach for lacto-fermentation. Cherries are subsequently depulped, fermented and washed before drying. Much like me, the finished cup is bright and outspoken with a great body.

Gonzalo Pablo Garcia inherited the land where his father grew corn back in 2018, and out of curiosity planted 600 coffee seedlings to see if he could successfully grow coffee at his high altitude, considering it’s also a somewhat cold microclimate. After 3 years of tending and waiting, his first return was disheartening- small beans of poor quality. Thankfully, Gonzalo reached out to an agronomist who advised him on how to properly fertilise the soil in his conditions, and things took a turn for the better.
Now he handles all of the farming and processing quite literally in-house with his family. They depulp the coffee on the farm to make it easier to reuse the cherry for fertiliser, then ferment and wash the coffee in plastic tanks in their house before being moved to the terrace to dry, tended to by the family turning the beans 3-4 daily over the course of 3 days.
We’re very grateful to be able to share this coffee with you, and hope you’ll appreciate it as we do with each sip.

It’s early October 1981, and there’s hardly a soul on Earth who hasn’t heard of you- after all, you’re smash hit rock stars with KILLER hair known world over as Queen. Bohemian Rhapsody, Somebody to Love, Don’t Stop Me Now, and Another One Bites the Dust have all topped the charts. Suddenly you look up, and David Bowie is barrelling toward you with his pile of Gold and Platinum records in tow, and BAM! You smash into each other and what comes of this collision??!! Under Pressure. An all time collaboration, and one of the most timeless hits to ever grace our ears.
You’re obviously on board with this, but surely you’re asking yourself by now “what are they going on about? What does the smash hit ‘Under Pressure’ have to do with this coffee?
Gesha. You know it. You love it. It’s a banger. A resilient and delicious Ethiopian varietal that’s been taken on a world tour.
Peru. I assume you know it, unless you’re learning your geography in the USA, in which case you’ve got enough problems as it is and we won’t pick on you. Peru is renowned for its crop cultivation and microclimates- developing literally thousands of varieties of potatoes is the stuff of legend.
This coffee is what happens when those two worlds collide. This coffee is Under Pressure. More specifically, and less metaphorically, this coffee is what is becoming known as “Inca Gesha” or sometimes “Native Gesha”- a unique mutation of Gesha cross-pollinating with other local varieties, resulting in a gorgeous and distinctly unique take on a classic.
Okay! You’ve piqued my interest, what does it taste like? Surprisingly sticky sweet for a Gesha, with berry jam and lemon-lime acidity, and some warm spices mulling about in the background. There’s a familiar florality and cleanliness to this new form of Gesha, but it's otherwise very unique and takes after the best of Peruvian coffee.

When I hear “semi-washed” it conjures up imagery of people in public bathrooms barely splashing their hands in the sink, even though there’s just no excuse for not knowing proper hand washing technique since Covid. Fortunately for all of us, this coffee has absolutely nothing to do with that, and I’m wondering why I’ve left that in the copy.
Semi-washed is used as a broadly recognizable term that can mean vastly different things as to how a coffee is actually processed. In this instance, it may be helpful to describe this lot as anaerobic washed. The coffee is first fermented anaerobically for 48 hours before then being depulped and fermented again in sealed bags in a water bath, with both the temperature and pH carefully controlled. After this second fermentation the coffee is semi-washed and then dried. The resulting cup is distinctly complex and clean, with loads of florals and a sticky berry sweetness.

https://friedhats.com/products/colombia-.lines:
Harvesting coffee is a laborious process; the diligent work of picking through thousands and thousands of cherries to pick at their ripest, from tree to tree until you’ve finished a long day of work. The timing of your hire is dependent on the readiness of a farmer to initiate harvest. The instability of this work creates an environment in which formal hire and employment is a gargantuan task. Because of this there is a cyclical element of disincentivizing reliable labor and professional expertise, and it only makes sense without well coordinated organization.
This is why Manos al Grano have teamed up with Azahar to create the Pickers Project. This is a team of 35 pickers and 20 farms (so far) who have banded together to create a system that works better for everyone involved. This gives farmers access to dedicated and skilled workers who are working in a system of full-time employment with fair wages, benefits, and compliance with labor laws- something that was near-impossible with the transient and informal nature of unreliable day-labor..
We are incredibly happy to be able to share coffee with you from this project once again- something that as we all support benefits everyone along the chain and improves the industry we all care about.

https://friedhats.com/products/colombia-.lines: The Colombia variety, or variedad Colombia, was introduced and implemented widespread across Colombia as a new disease-resistant varietal to preempt the imminent outbreak of the coffee rust virus in 1982. The disease landed in the Americas in the 1970s, and the fear of the entire coffee agricultural sector collapsing across a given country was very real. Cenicafe developed this caturra x timor hybrid and is largely credited with staving off the spread of the virus for decades. Nearly 30 years later Colombia was largely replaced by the newer Castillo, specifically engineered to be coffee rust resistant, more effective than the generically disease-resistant Colombia that over time proved to be largely rust resistant rather than totally resistant. Brief history lesson aside, some producers have elected to continue producing the Colombia variety to great success, David Dagua being a prime example. A variety largely grown and subsequently replaced out of pragmatism, there’s something heartening about tasting and sharing a particularly nice lot of Colombia being well produced today.

https://friedhats.com/products/rwanda-sh.lines: While “anoxic pillow” sounds like a targeted ad that I get on instagram now that I’m in my 30s with back problems, it’s actually a brilliant way of simplifying advanced processing for coffee. Typically, creating an oxygen-free environment for fermentation to occur that also regulates temperature involves a lot of brewing-type equipment– stainless steel vats, pressure and heat regulators and the like, all of which cost good money. To lower the barrier of entry, along comes the ‘anoxic pillow’ method, brilliant in its simplicity. The cherries fill a container, then a sheet is placed over the top large enough to cover it in its entirety, and pour water on top. That’s it. The weight of the water pushes the oxygen out and seals the sheet across the top, not allowing any fresh oxygen in. As the fermentation begins and the temperature rises, the water acts as a heat transfer, automatically cooling it down. No fancy tech, just the fundamentals of fermentation.

A couple times in the past we were lucky enough to showcase coffee from Gabriel Castaño, a local legend known colloquially as southern Huila’s “Godfather” of Pink Bourbon. When he found this varietal that was both delicious and resistant to coffee rust, he replanted his entire farm and sung its praises to any who would listen, pushing fellow producers to follow suit to the extent that many neighbors simply referred to the varietal as “Castaño.”
As you may have noticed, Gabriel is not the producer of this lot this year. Our hearts go out to the Castaño family for the great loss they have sustained, as the torch passes to the next generation and Jefferson continues the work of his father. We share this coffee with an immense amount of respect and gratitude, and with an understanding that coffee is more than just a product– it is legacy, livelihood, and an enduring memory all coming together that we have the privilege to share.

Maria has been around coffee her entire life- the child of coffee growers, she worked as a coffee quality analyst in Cauca before making the turn back to coffee production. After picking and sorting, the coffee undergoes a 24 hour pre-fermentation in cherry, followed by a 36 hour anaerobic fermentation with mucilage before being dried. This is another example of what we've been speaking to of late, with processing becoming more complex and not falling neatly into the same boxes they used to. This coffee is called "semi-washed,” but we're finding it more useful to share more specific processing information so the catch-all terms don't leave you lacking information.

OoooOOOooooohhhhh it’s an exciting day- another new origin for us at Friedhats! That means new flavors, new roast profiles, cute new artwork from Ivo- what’s not to love?
Andean Mountain Range, predominantly Saraguro Formation (flows into the Pacific Ocean)
Landowners include: Segundo Cartuche | Jaime Cartuche | Gustavo Cartuche | Gonzalo Armijos | Isauro Salinas | Baltazar Contento | Patricio Suquilanda | Guillermo Armijos | Mesias Sandoval Climate
One of the most remarkable characteristics of HLP is that all of the coffee is irrigated. This is thanks to both the perennial waterfall, Cascada San Pablo, that sits above the estate and the ingenuity of the fertilization system Juan employs. Fertilizers are mixed in controlled amounts with water. Most established lots are fertilized 4 days a week and 1 day with just water.
Juan chooses to replace trees when necessary instead of stumping. Because of the irrigation system, the length of time for new trees to reach production is the same as that of stumped trees. He has an extensive nursery on site which serves to both regenerate existing blocks and nurture new varietals for future lots.

So obviously we’ve got these general labels that we use to launch different coffees from different origins. We’ve got 4 variations of the Ethiopia label, and 3 variations of the Colombia label. The more variety we have in labels, the more stuck in our own ways we get about what goes in which label, this unspoken rule that we get very set on over time, and genuinely have no idea whether anyone outside of the roastery thinks the same way about things. This label (the red/pink Colombia) we use for funky and fruit forward naturals. Insider info.
This coffee is a perfect example of what we’re looking for when we think about this label. Grown by Eliana Bravo at La Esmeralda, then processed by Sigilo. They put the cherries into a tank to control the PH and temperature. For 98 hours the coffee ferments, with the mosto removed every 12 hours to be cooled and be reintroduced to regulate the fermentation. Then the coffee is dried on raised beds for 15 days until the moisture level is stable. And then they ship it and then we roast it and then you drink it and then you feel happy. And that makes me happy. I love you.

A washed Kenya, fresh harvest from Kiangoi Factory washing station. Clean and fruity.
SL 34 does so much of the heavy lifting in the specialty coffee world in Kenya, and understandably so– the distinctive blackcurrant and winey acidity is practically synonymous with Kenyan coffee. Its origin story is so interesting that it deserves its own blog post (coming soon), but the tagline basically boils down to this: colonial missions sowed the seeds of capitalist exploitation more than truth? Shocking, surprising, and dare I say, scandalous? To be continued. Anyways. The enduring legacy of SL 34 is one that we should be deeply grateful for, and appreciative of each and every time we get to drink it. Compared to more modern varieties it is far more susceptible to disease and has a substantively lower yield, but the gulf in quality is astonishing. So while it makes sense to want to buy and drink this brilliant variety, it makes increasingly less sense to grow it from a labor and risk perspective. While many larger estates have moved on to higher yielding and more disease resistant varieties, we’re grateful for every producer carrying the flame of SL 34.

This particular lot comes from Nyabirongo, nestled in the southern slopes of the Rwenzori Mountains in western Uganda, bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo. Bakanzo smallholders cultivate SL14 and SL28, varieties you may recognize as being predominantly found in Kenyan coffee. The SLs, SL28 in particular, are very susceptible to CBD and nematodes, have low yields, but have the potential to produce stellar cups, making them a high-risk high-reward proposition to grow. Smallholders deliver ripe cherries to the Nyabirongo factory where they are sun-dried on raised African beds, providing us the chance to have a stellar natural processed SL28, something we do not often experience with Kenyan SL28 almost exclusively being washed.

Leon’s grandparents moved from Greece to Tanzania in the early 1900s and began what is now the family legacy of working in coffee. He came up amidst parents and grandparents growing coffee on low-altitude land before he took intrigue with specialty coffee in the 2000s and began searching for something at a higher altitude better suited to producing higher quality coffee. In 2007 the journey of Acacia Hills started with Leon rebuilding a dilapidated farm and planting SL28, Gesha, and Pacamara. In the time since, Acacia Hills has won private auctions in Tanzania with its gesha lots, making Leon one of the forerunners for bringing about higher quality and rare varietals to the country.
Tanzania has an important chapter in the story of gesha. After its discovery in Ethiopia, gesha was taken to the Lyamangu Coffee Research Station in Tanzania, where the plants were successfully cultivated and subsequently distributed throughout Central America. Despite the fact that Tanzania played a pivotal role in the now global cultivation of gesha, its prominence in Tanzania remains very low.

https://friedhats.com/products/colombia-.lines: The Colombia variety, or variedad Colombia, was introduced and implemented widespread across Colombia as a new disease-resistant varietal to preempt the imminent outbreak of the coffee rust virus in 1982. The disease landed in the Americas in the 1970s, and the fear of the entire coffee agricultural sector collapsing across a given country was very real. Cenicafe developed this caturra x timor hybrid and is largely credited with staving off the spread of the virus for decades. Nearly 30 years later Colombia was largely replaced by the newer Castillo, specifically engineered to be coffee rust resistant, more effective than the generically disease-resistant Colombia that over time proved to be largely rust resistant rather than totally resistant. Brief history lesson aside, some producers have elected to continue producing the Colombia variety to great success, David Dagua being a prime example. A variety largely grown and subsequently replaced out of pragmatism, there’s something heartening about tasting and sharing a particularly nice lot of Colombia being well produced today.

The first release from La Maria this year is an aerobic natural– coffee placed in grainpro bags to ferment for a few days before drying. https://friedhats.com/products/ethiopia-.lines:
Many people familiar with cooking know that a splash of pineapple will act as a tenderizer for meats in a marinade. The magic component here lies within both the flesh and stem of the pineapple- an enzyme known as bromelain. Bromelain accelerates the breakdown of protein compounds, hence its reputation as a tenderizer. In the past few years it has become a relatively common addition to coffee ferments for the same reason: when bromelain is introduced to coffee cherries it accelerates the release of mucus from the cherry (that sentence felt gross to write).
Interestingly, pineapple fermentation is being studied and experimented with more and more in Indonesia especially with robusta, as a means of reducing caffeine content which is substantially higher in robusta than arabica. The fermentation process with the addition of bromelain causes a breakdown of the proteins in cell walls so that, in time, caffeine will dissolve into water. Any reduction in caffeine content is also a reduction in bitterness, leading to an increase in clarity and perceived sweetness, enhancing the taste experience of the cup.
This lot is processed first with the whole cherry fermented in sealed tanks together with pineapple, carried out for 5-10 days. After fermentation is deemed to be finished the coffee is moved to raised beds to sun dry. The finished cup has a pronounced sweetness and clarity for this amount of processing, bursting pink grapefruit, lychee and sweet tea.

Some of you may be clued in by now that there are generally a handful of varieties that show up in most Kenyan coffees. Mixed varieties are very common because there are usually many hundreds of smallholders delivering cherry to a factory for processing. Want to get in the weeds just a little bit about these common Kenyan varieties? I don’t know why I framed that as a question, it’s happening, you just don’t have to read it I guess.
SL28 & SL34 are both “Scott Lab” varieties, varieties selected for study by the British Colonial Scott Agricultural Laboratories during the 1930s. Both are notable for their exceptional cup quality, low yields, and risk for CBD and rust. Beyond tasting stellar, SL28 is remarkable for its rusticity, meaning it can be left untended for years or even decades before returning to successful production. Because of this there are many documented SL28 trees that are 80 years old and still productive. SL34 is one of these contested origin stories that sometime we may have to dive more deeply into. Collected from a single tree on Loresho Estate in Kabete, it was called “French Mission” with the understanding that it was a bourbon by way of, you guessed it, French missionaries. Modern genetic testing has shown this to be untrue, with all signs pointing to it being related to the Typica genetic. Makes you wonder about what else these missionaries are lying about. Last but not least (or as the missionaries would say, the least will be last or something like that), Batian. A composite variety bred by the Coffee Research Foundation in Kenya, it’s composed of SL28, SL34, Sudan Rume, N39, K7, SL4, and Timor Hybrid. This genetic cocktail greatly increased its disease resistances along with a significant boost to its yield potential without sacrificing much in the way of cup quality, making it an excellent variety for smallholders to cultivate.

We just had the washed version of this coffee, and before that the natural, and now we come in here saying shit like “hybrid washed” and I know some of you think I’m making that up. Well I have bad news for you, skeptics– everything is made up. But that doesn’t make it meaningless. Meaningless is the time I wasted in therapy. Hybrid washed means something for real. For this lot it means after harvest the cherries start first with a 14 hour open-tank fermentation, before undergoing a further 18 hour fermentation in an oxygen-free environment. After this fermentation stage the coffee is depulped, fermented aerobically again, then washed and dried. Hybrid washed is the shorthand way of saying “kind of a complex fermentation, but ultimately washed.”

https://friedhats.com/products/panama-au.lines:
Panamanian coffee has a tremendously outsized role in specialty coffee relative to its production volume; the gesha of Panama, whispered about in awe as auction sites crash processing five-figure bids for prized lots, meanwhile it makes up only one tenth of one percent of global coffee production. Over the past two decades, the alluring Panamanian gesha has become the muse, the darling, the “draw me like one of your French girls” of specialty coffee. But it wasn’t always like that…
After being introduced to the Americas in the 1950s, gesha was distributed across Panama in the 1960s as a rust-resistant variety. It did not catch on well with many farmers as it proved… difficult. Finicky to grow, low yield, a smaller harvest window, and particular about processing in a time where outstanding quality did little to line your pocket relative to simply producing in volume, it’s a wonder anyone kept growing the newly introduced variety.
In time it became clear that the qualitative difference between gesha grown at low altitude and high altitude was staggering, causing some to take note. The true big break would come when Hacienda La Esmerelda began isolating gesha-only lots, which yielded a staggering $20.10 per pound at the best of Panama auction in 2004. This snowball has grown to an avalanche as the scramble for Panama gesha far outpaces the ability and even possibility to grow more at a certain point, leading to an exponential growth in price that was nearly 700x that 2004 price last year, and will certainly hurt my feelings and cause me to question a lot again this year. Seriously, $30.000 per kilo. Anyways, this lot is great and apparently relatively cheap. Just remember, it could have been thirty thousand.

https://friedhats.com/products/ethiopia-.lines:
It’s about time we put together a comprehensive processing guide to refer to, but until then let’s revisit what honey processing is. Cutting right to the chase, honey processing basically sits somewhere on the spectrum between washed and natural, but isn’t quite either. To start, the cherry to some varying degree is removed, leaving differing amounts of mucilage on the bean. Then the coffee is dried in the style of a natural, requiring different amounts of time or drying styles depending on mucilage amounts. Simple enough. Lighter colors like white or yellow generally have the least amount of mucilage left, making the processing simple and clean, closer to a washed process– usually bright and floral. Conversely, darker colors like red or black tend to have more mucilage, then get dried slowly in the shade or (relatively) quicker in the sun resulting in different colors from the dried residue– such as black or red. Makes sense!
There’s the old saying “you can lead a horse to water, but you can’t make him drink.” Well I’ve never spent much time around horses, but I think I’ve given you enough information to understand what a red honey processed coffee is. So drink it up.

The longer maturation period is apparent in the quality and complexity of the coffee, making it my exact opposite (me being immature, low quality, and lacking any sort of depth according to the last few dates I went on). Well there I go, making everything about me again, I guess they were right and I have some serious reflecting to do. But don’t let my epiphany here take away from the ultimate point of this little write-up: Danche is an absolute banger of an Ethiopia nat, and there’s a reason we keep working with SNAP at their various washing stations. They do excellent work in processing and agronomy, and go through the rigmarole of organic certification on principle. We’re thrilled to have this coffee, and I just know that you will be too.

https://friedhats.com/products/ethiopia-.lines:
Always interested in fun information to share about a coffee or an interesting angle to write about, something that always stands out with an Ethiopian coffee is an entire lot comprised of one named variety. That’s a rarity. So upon digging in a bit on wolisho, my head began to spin. But let’s start easy, with what we know. We know that it’s a landrace selection– meaning that it naturally evolved in a certain microregion, and was eventually selected for propagation after finding some favor amongst growers. We know it’s largely grown across Gedeo, Guji, and Sidama. We know it does well at very high altitudes, and can produce a stellar cup.
What makes wolisho very interesting to me is that it highlights the difficulties of documenting and categorizing landrace varieties. Named after a similar-looking non-coffee tree, wolisho, tracing the fractals of the same name across regions, languages and dialects would require quite the undertaking. For instance, when talking about named landrace varieties in this area with three primary languages, one quickly amasses all of: waliso, walancho, welencho, wecincho, awicho, gantincho, gidicho, kolisho, kolinsho– all in addition to the commonly accepted variations of the same coffee: wolisho, walisho, walichu, and welicho.
So, while the scope of identifying and categorizing landrace varieties may be a fascinating but confusing road to walk, I’ll tell you one thing for sure that no one is confused about: how this coffee tastes. We loved this lot so much last year that it was one of the first coffees we booked in for this year, certain that it would live up to our expectations– and wow, was that a good bet.

https://friedhats.com/products/ethiopia-.lines:
You may see the specificity of Gesha 1931 and have questions about the difference, if there is any, between simply Gesha and Gesha 1931. It’s a keen observation, and a great question– let’s break it down a bit. Gesha is the name of the variety that exploded to prominence at the Best of Panama competition in 2004, shaping much of the way specialty coffee has evolved for the last two decades. The short and sweet of it is that this variety was harvested by a Consul of the British Empire in Ethiopia tasked with collecting coffee seeds from around Gesha Mountain in 1931. From there these beans made their way to the Director of Agriculture in Kenya, down to Tanzania, over to Costa Rica, then ultimately to Panama where the full potential of this variety would be realized.
Three years after the emergence of Gesha on the global scene as the prize of Hacienda La Esmeralda, the founders of Gesha Village set out to recontextualize this now celebrated variety. Leasing a plot of land near the Gori Gesha Forest, they went on a search of their own through the forest to make a selection of coffee that was the best match for what had become famous as Panamanian Gesha. After analyzing the plant morphology, bean shape and size, and the cupping profile most of all, they landed on this selection that is now known as Gesha 1931– named for the year the acclaimed variety was first harvested from the forest.

This exceptional lot is composed entirely of a small-screen coffee variety,
mostly graded to a precise screen size of 13. The inherent density and
compact cellular structure of these smaller beans result in a highly

Our process initiates with a rigorous selection protocol: we combine
precisely 90% optimally ripe cherries with a 10% over-ripe allocation to
introduce structural depth and complexity. Following an initial buoyancy
separation in water to eliminate defective fruit, the selected cherries
undergo a controlled four-hour hydration soak, optimizing them for
subsequent refinement phases.
To fully preserve their intricate flavor profiles, our cherries undergo a
meticulous, 35-day slow-drying process on elevated beds. By limiting each
bed to a single, 25kg layer of fruit and positioning them in shaded, highly
ventilated environments, we harness low-temperature, high-airflow
dynamics. This artisanal method ensures an exceptionally gentle and
uniform dehydration.

https://friedhats.com/products/ethiopia-.lines:
It’s about time we put together a comprehensive processing guide to refer to, but until then let’s revisit what honey processing is. Cutting right to the chase, honey processing basically sits somewhere on the spectrum between washed and natural, but isn’t quite either. To start, the cherry to some varying degree is removed, leaving differing amounts of mucilage on the bean. Then the coffee is dried in the style of a natural, requiring different amounts of time or drying styles depending on mucilage amounts. Simple enough. Lighter colors like white or yellow generally have the least amount of mucilage left, making the processing simple and clean, closer to a washed process– usually bright and floral. Conversely, darker colors like red or black tend to have more mucilage, then get dried slowly in the shade or (relatively) quicker in the sun resulting in different colors from the dried residue– such as black or red. Makes sense!
There’s the old saying “you can lead a horse to water, but you can’t make him drink.” Well I’ve never spent much time around horses, but I think I’ve given you enough information to understand what a black honey processed coffee is. So drink it up.

https://friedhats.com/products/kenya-run.lines:
Kenya washed (harvest 2026)
On Tuesdays, and also on other days, I like to give myself and others around me a dilemma. So here’s what I came up with: you either have to drink a strawberry-matcha-latte next to every cup of Kenya for the rest of your life. Or, you can never drink Kenya ever again.
Now, while the thought of never ever drinking Kenya ever again horrifies me to my bones, the thought of having to drink a strawberry-mmma… no there’s just no way.
Luckily, I didn’t have to choose so I continued with introducing our latest Kenya-arrival.
It’s from the Kirinyaga region, located on the south slopes of mount Kenya.
Smallholders pick their cherries at 1700-1800 masl and deliver to the Kiangoi Coffee Factory which is part of the Rung’eto Farmers cooperative society.
The varieties used are SL28 and SL34 and the coffee is fully washed. It’s imported by Nordic Approach, where we usually get a lot of our Kenyan coffees from.
In the cup you will get a bright and sweet coffee with a punchy acidity. It has a juicy and syrupy texture with some molasses and flavors of lemon tea, rhubarb, apricots and blackberries in the finish
